architecture.approach: One authorization pipeline, declared in the router and never re-implemented in a controller (CON-105, CON-512): server/src/routes/workspaceRoutes.ts declares `protect` then `requirePermission('<area>:<action>')` per route, the middleware resolves the workspace from the URL slug plus membership and attaches req.workspace, req.role and req.permissions, and the controller reads the workspace from that request object so every query is scoped to req.workspace._id (CON-106). Permissions are a closed catalogue in server/src/config/permissions.ts; roles are either the five seeded system roles (isSystem true, workspaceId null) or custom roles owned by one workspace. All role resolution and granting goes through server/src/utils/roleAccess.ts so the privilege ceiling lives in one testable module, and pure helpers (roleHelpers, workspaceHelpers, roleRank) stay free of HTTP and the database (CON-109).

fields.name: members
fields.type: array of { user: ObjectId, roleId: ObjectId, joinedAt: Date }

dataModel.flowDescription: A signed-in user creates a workspace: the document is written with the creator as owner and as the first member holding the Product Owner role id, plus a unique slug and a 12-hex invite code, and the user's workspace list and activeWorkspace are updated. Every later request to /api/workspaces/:slug/... resolves membership through requirePermission, which attaches the workspace, the role and the permission keys, so controllers only ever act inside that workspace. Membership changes (join by code, invite/accept, role change, removal, leave) all funnel through roleAccess: findAssignableRole restricts the target to a system role or a role of the same workspace, canGrantRole compares the actor's permissions with the role's unless the actor owns the workspace, and findDefaultRole supplies Viewer for invite-code joins. Roles live either as system documents (workspaceId null, isSystem true) or as custom documents owned by one workspace with a partial unique index on { workspaceId, name }.

securityConsiderations.description: requirePermission resolves the workspace with slug equality AND 'members.user': the caller's ObjectId, so a non-member can never learn that a workspace exists. On success the controller uses req.workspace, and CON-106 makes 'filter by req.workspace._id' the review rule for every new workspace query.

findAssignableRole is the only way a role id from a request becomes a role document: it requires a valid ObjectId string and matches { _id, $or: [{ isSystem: true }, { workspaceId }] }, so a role of another workspace cannot be granted. canGrantRole then compares permission sets and always refuses Product Owner for a non-owner, which makes self-promotion and lateral escalation fail closed.

Non-string and malformed identifiers are rejected before any query runs (findAssignableRole returns null, findCustomRoleOr404 answers 404), which prevents operator payloads such as { "$ne": null } from widening a lookup (CON-516).

permissionMiddleware.test.ts asserts the 401/400/403 branches and the attached context, rbacSecurity.test.ts asserts the privilege ceiling with the real SYSTEM_ROLES catalogue, and rbac.test.ts plus workspaces.test.ts exercise the same rules over HTTP against a real database, so a regression in the pipeline fails the build (CON-402).

performanceConsiderations.strategy: Each authorized request costs one indexed Workspace lookup (index on members.user plus the unique slug) and one Role.findById; the same document is reused by the controller instead of being re-queried.
getMyWorkspaces projects name, slug, owner, members and createdAt and populates only member names and role names, so the workspace switcher never ships invite codes, emails or full user documents.
Role documents are shared across workspaces for the system roles (one document per role, workspaceId null) so role resolution stays a single indexed lookup rather than a per-workspace copy.

risks.description: A future workspace route is added without requirePermission
risks.mitigation: The permission is declared next to the path in workspaceRoutes.ts, and the middleware and integration suites fail when the pipeline changes

risks.description: Legacy members without a roleId break access after a migration
risks.mitigation: repairMemberRoles runs on boot, getCurrentUser self-heals on demand, and the middleware answers an explicit 403 instead of crashing

risks.description: A custom role is deleted while still assigned
risks.mitigation: deleteCustomRole checks Workspace.exists({ 'members.roleId': role._id }) and answers 409

risks.description: An invite code leaks to the wrong audience
risks.mitigation: Codes grant the read-only Viewer role only, can be rotated by settings:manage, and the join route is rate limited
